records.subsection: Which models are underlying the GSA specific model?
records.finding: ISW is analysed with a numerical integrated model. The GSP never uses the analytical/numerical/statistical vocabulary, so the classification is inferred from the model description; no analytical depletion-factor or statistical component appears anywhere.

records.notes: Classification inferred, not stated by the GSP; basis recorded in the notes.

records.subsection: Based on the model calculation, what amount of ISW depletion is recorded as a result of pumping specifically?
records.finding: Depletion volumes are produced by differencing a calibrated historical simulation against a counterfactual no-pumping simulation, yielding 504,400 AFY of in-Subbasin depletion plus 141,800 AFY of increased subsurface inflow, disaggregated by reach, neighbouring subbasin, month and water-year type.
records.direct_quote: "Depletions were quantified through a modeling exercise to isolate the impacts of pumping on interconnected surface waters. The historical conditions simulation of the MercedWRM was used together with a newly developed simulation that removed pumping from the Merced Subbasin... Stream depletion was calculated by obtaining the difference in the stream-groundwater flow with and without groundwater pumping." — GSP §2.2.7, p. 2-193 [PDF 284]

records.subsection: What specific value is pointed to for achieving sustainability?
records.finding: No ISW-specific minimum threshold, measurable objective or trigger exists. All ISW criteria are inherited wholesale from the chronic lowering of groundwater levels indicator under the §354.36 proxy.

records.subsection: Riparian ET exempted from accounting
records.finding: Riparian Areas are permanently Inactive, so their evapotranspiration is never debited against any allocation — while the acreage continues to earn allocation. records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.section_source: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.subsection: How is the attribution of depletion carried out across space?
records.finding: 141,800 AFY of increased subsurface inflow from neighbouring subbasins is explicitly booked outside the Subbasin's own accounts. Interbasin MOUs exist but no mechanism reconciles the two sides of a shared boundary into a single depletion account.
records.direct_quote: "These impacts will eventually result in depletions, but because they occur outside of the Merced Subbasin they are accounted separately" — GSP §2.2.7, p. 2-195 [PDF 286]

records.subsection: How are you attributing depletion to a specific pump?
records.finding: The all-or-nothing paired simulation structurally sidesteps the superposition error but cannot attribute depletion to any individual well, field or GSA. Private agricultural pumping is element-averaged in IWFM, so per-well attribution is unavailable at current model resolution, not merely unperformed.

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?
records.finding: There is no combined accounting approach, common metric, stacking methodology or rule against double-counting a single physical outcome across categories — while the scoring explicitly rewards stacking.
records.direct_quote: Searched the MLRP RFP and Application — "Projects that address multiple Priority Criteria Categories will score higher than projects that address only one" (Application p. 10 [PDF 18]), and the rubric permits the same acreage to be claimed under DAC, Ecological and Geographic Prioritization simultaneously. The output is a point total, not quantities in different units.
records.notes: Merced's one working co-benefit mechanism achieves integrity by unbundling (ring-fencing habitat water), not by stacking — worth surfacing as a design tension.

records.subsection: What specific value is pointed to for achieving sustainability?
records.finding: Two independent commenters — an NGO coalition and a federal fisheries agency — asked for a biological definition of the ISW undesirable result, and neither got one. The ecological question is externalised to the surface-water regulatory regime administered by the irrigation districts, which are themselves GSA member agencies.
records.direct_quote: Searched GSP §6.8 (ISW SMC) and the two places in Appendix F-15 Attachment C where a biological endpoint was requested (NGO Coalition, p. 8 of 19 [PDF 1260]; NMFS, p. 2 of 19 [PDF 1254]) — no biological or ecological criterion is adopted anywhere for the ISW indicator. Both responses point instead to existing GSP sections describing concerns and to instream flow requirements administered by the irrigation districts; a third routes to an ongoing Programmatic EIR.
records.notes: Name the pattern: ecological sufficiency by regulatory reference. It also means the ISW indicator has no ecological endpoint of its own that could ever be measured.

records.notes: The response says the location "will be considered", not that it was adopted — do not assert the causal link without checking installed well coordinates against the reach. | Also touches 1.4 Measurement Methods (monitoring-network placement).

records.subsection: What specific value is pointed to for achieving sustainability?
records.finding: The assumption doing the most work in the whole ISW chapter is that pre-2015 conditions need not be corrected — stated flatly and never analysed. The Merced River was already net losing historically, so the baseline against which improvement is measured already contains substantial depletion.
records.direct_quote: "GSAs are not required to correct undesirable results that occurred prior to January 1, 2015... The Joint TACs want to keep these conditions from getting worse in the future." — GSP §6.8.1.1, p. 6-75 [PDF 449]
records.notes: Two verbatim variants of the statutory limit exist in the comment record (PDF 1254 vs PDF 1259) and must not be merged into one sentence.

records.subsection: Is the concern of differing depletion at varying aquifer depths recognized?
records.finding: The ISW network deliberately excludes the sub-Corcoran Western Lower aquifer on the reasoning that shallow systems are the connected ones — but within the shallow network the wells are screened hundreds of feet below the water table and vertical gradient data are unavailable.
records.direct_quote: "It is recognized that these screen intervals are relatively deep and measured vertical gradient data are not available" — GSP §7.1.6.2, p. 7-11 [PDF 476]
records.notes: The ETTSS nested clusters are the direct fix.

records.subsection: What other incentive programs exist for land repurposing?
records.finding: ETSGSA runs a non-multibenefit control programme alongside the MLRP and states in its own words what the multibenefit premium buys: duration and a co-benefit obligation. It is running the counterfactual next to the treatment.

records.notes: The single most useful sentence in the Turlock MLRP corpus for the DWR recommendation.

records.subsection: How is water savings calculated?
records.finding: The 2024 land-suitability assessment estimates demand reduction per practice from remote-sensing ET applied to a GIS-derived suitable area — 44,808 AF across six practices, 17,112 irrigated acres. These are suitability estimates, not enrolled, contracted or achieved acreage.
records.direct_quote: "The demand reduction was calculated from the long-term evapotranspiration (ET) dataset and utilized as a proxy for groundwater extraction by pumping. Two datasets from CalETa and LandIQ ET were utilized to calculate the irrigation season ET for each MLRP practice implementation area." — Technical Memorandum §2.1, p. 15 [PDF 15]
records.notes: The table header reads "(Acft)" with no time unit; the annual basis was confirmed arithmetically (6,107 ac x 2.7 ft = 16,489 AF), not assumed.

records.subsection: How is water savings calculated?
records.finding: The siting method is quantitative and auditable — named thresholds (200 m stream buffer, 0.1 degree slope, 10 m DEM), named public datasets, an iterative overlay, and an aerial-imagery ground-truthing step.
records.direct_quote: "The landscape characteristics identified as suitable for floodplain reconnection was defined as all land within 200 meters of an identified stream with a land slope of 0.1 degree or less… The National Hydrography Dataset (NHD; USGS 2023) was used to identify all perennial and intermittent drainage lines within ETSGSA." — Appendix K §5.1.1, pp. 25–26 [PDF 1375–1376]
records.notes: Rigour is concentrated at siting, not at verification — the cleanest single statement of the MLRP accounting problem in this project, and it is Turlock's own design.

records.subsection: What are the requirements for monitoring water savings and co-benefits of land repurposing?
records.finding: The MLRP's own monitoring does not measure water savings at all. Its two always-required activities are a Photo Log and a Conditions Description; the quantitative add-ons measure recharge inputs and ponding, not demand reduction.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary search of the Implementation Monitoring Plan returns zero occurrences of "evapotranspiration", "ET data", "LandIQ" and "consumptive use". Appendix A Project-Specific Monitoring Checklist marks Photo Log and Conditions Description "Yes" at every phase; all quantitative items are per-project "Yes / No".
records.notes: MLRP project monitoring verifies that the project was built and persists; the accounting platform separately measures whether consumptive use fell.

records.subsection: Who is included in water savings tracking?

records.subsection: Is dust considered in MLRP projects?
records.finding: In Turlock dust is a landowner liability, not a programme benefit — the inverse of the framing the co-benefit literature assumes. Every appearance frames dust as a nuisance to be avoided, and the one place it appears as a benefit is an explicitly optional best practice.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary searches: dust appears 10 times across the Implementation Standards, 0 times in GSP Chapter 8, once in the Annual Report. "Decreased particulate and other air emissions" (Vegetated Cover, p. 1) is the only particulate reference in the entire MLRP corpus, with no measurement method.
records.notes: Confirms the two-basin dust gap in a stronger form than "no method exists": the agencies conceptualise the relationship in the opposite direction.

records.subsection: Once a parcel stops pumping, does its paper entitlement to pump get freed up?

records.subsection: Can the freed entitlement be used elsewhere in the basin?

records.notes: "Transfer" is "[to be determined]" in both rule versions and §6.02 softened from "intends to develop" to "will consider development of" — a design state, not a policy commitment.

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?
records.finding: Co-benefits are accounted separately at planning scale for the subset with an available method, with the unmethodded remainder explicitly disclaimed — a published non-inventory of uncounted co-benefits, which is what makes a co-benefit claim auditable.
records.direct_quote: "We also expect an recharge benefits to result from orchard swale rewilding, restoration of pre-development hydrology, floodplain reconnection and flood flow dispersal and retention; however, recharge from those practices has not yet been estimated and was not included in this analysis." — Appendix K §5.1.1, p. 28 [PDF 1378] [sic — "an recharge benefits"]
records.notes: Separation exists exactly where it is cheapest (ex ante, GIS-and-model) and vanishes where it would cost something (ex post, per project). The stack is also unstable between documents.

records.subsection: Which of the three dimensions does each basin's documentation actually address, and which is structurally absent?
records.finding: Asked three times to prevent racially disparate impact in the SMCs, the GSAs answered each time that uniform methodology is equitable outcome — a procedural-equity answer to a distributional-equity question.
records.direct_quote: "MTs and MOs are established with the same methodology throughout the entire Subbasin and are no higher or lower in the various communities across the Subbasin. Given that disadvantaged communities cover most of the Subbasin (including areas containing about 82 percent of the Subbasin population), consistently-determined sustainable management criteria are applied in an equitable manner." — Attachment C, p. 13 of 19 [PDF 1265]
records.notes: Fairness requirement: the GSAs' claim that they monitor DACs is verifiable and true; what is contested is whether uniform criteria can be assumed equitable without checking.

records.subsection: What specific value is pointed to for achieving sustainability?
records.finding: HEADLINE. The 2020 GSP set a volumetric ISW minimum threshold (69,700 AF/yr, MO and all interim milestones identical). Amendment 1 replaced it entirely with a groundwater-elevation proxy at shallow wells. The stated reason is operational, not scientific: the model could not be run annually. This is the only instance in the three-basin study of a GSA adopting volumetric ISW accounting and then formally abandoning it.
records.direct_quote: "The 2020 GSP based depletion on a modeled quantity; however, it is unrealistic that the SVIHM will be updated annually to make this determination. GSP Amendment 1 aligns with the approach of the 2022 Salinas Valley GSPs that monitors depletion of ISW by proxy through shallow groundwater levels near locations of interconnection." (Periodic Evaluation 2.7.1, PDF p78)
records.notes: MOST GAP-RELEVANT SENTENCE IN THE SALINAS VALLEY SET. The binding constraint on volumetric ISW accounting was the cost/feasibility of running the model every year. GAP is an annual accounting platform - this is a direct argument for what GAP could change. | Also touches 1.8 (the model output no longer feeds any criterion after the proxy substitution).

records.subsection: Is the compliance loop (modeling and estimation outputs that translate into thresholds, then into policy, then into outcomes that feed policy) closed?
records.finding: SHARPEST FRAMING OF THE BASIN. The 2020 GSP named the missing no-pumping simulation as the specific reason its threshold could not be attributed to pumping. Amendment 1 performed exactly that simulation - and in the same document replaced the volumetric criterion with an elevation proxy rather than re-setting the criterion to the newly attributable number. The capability the GSA said it lacked arrived, and the criterion it would have supported was withdrawn instead of corrected.
records.direct_quote: Amendment 1 Table 5-7 presents the paired-simulation result (2,600 / 5,800 AF/yr); Amendment 1 8.11.2 sets the MT by elevation proxy. No provision anywhere in Amendment 1 ties the Table 5-7 output to any threshold, trigger, or annual determination. Verified by full-text review of chapter 8.
records.notes: Distinct from Merced (never had an ISW criterion to lose) and from East Turlock (kept criteria, could not attribute). Salinas Valley achieved attribution and retired the criterion it could have anchored.

records.subsection: What specific value is pointed to for achieving sustainability?
records.finding: Reservoir conservation releases are excluded from threshold applicability entirely, on the reasoning that depleting deliberately-released recharge water is the intended outcome. Defensible and clearly reasoned - but the Salinas River is reservoir-dominated in exactly the summer months when pumping peaks, and no document quantifies how much of the year or of the interconnected reach-length falls inside the carve-out.
records.direct_quote: "No minimum thresholds are established for times when flow in a river is due to conservation releases from a reservoir. One purpose for these conservation releases is to recharge the Salinas Valley Groundwater Basin. Therefore, depletion of conservation releases is a desired outcome, and the minimum thresholds and measurable objectives do not apply to these flows." (Amendment 1 8.11.2, PDF p325)
records.notes: Record as an UNQUANTIFIED exclusion, not an improper one. Genuinely transferable design question for GAP: how should an accounting platform treat managed recharge releases in an ISW ledger? Restated at Periodic Evaluation 2.7.3 (PDF p81).

records.subsection: Is the compliance loop (modeling and estimation outputs that translate into thresholds, then into policy, then into outcomes that feed policy) closed?
records.finding: Because the ISW MT is set numerically identical to the groundwater-level MT, the GSA reasons that ISW cannot have impacted groundwater levels. True as arithmetic and vacuous as accounting: an indicator defined as identical to another can never diverge from it, so it can never independently signal anything.
records.direct_quote: "Depletion of ISW is measured by proxy using groundwater elevations, and the SMC are set at the same levels as the groundwater level SMC. Therefore, depletion of ISW has not impacted groundwater levels." (Periodic Evaluation 2.7.4, PDF p81)
records.notes: The same construction recurs for every other indicator in 2.7.4. This is the precise mechanism guaranteeing the ISW indicator produces no information the groundwater-level indicator did not already produce. Structurally the same as Merced (ISW rides the level proxy passively) but stated more explicitly here.

records.subsection: What approach or combination of approaches is used to measure depletion of interconnected surface water? (field measurements & models)
records.finding: The most sophisticated ISW FIELD work in the three-basin corpus: five independent direct-measurement methods applied to a 6-mile reach, producing quantified sub-reach seepage rates and hydraulic conductivities. Nothing comparable exists in the Merced or East Turlock document sets.
records.direct_quote: "A variety of field methods were then implemented to evaluate river seepage rates within the Somavia Reach: a) high-precision synoptic-flow surveys to detail flow losses through the reach; b) streamflow gaging to assess seasonal sub-reach losses; c) shallow piezometer clusters to assess seasonal changes to vertical head gradients; d) riverbed temperature profiler time-series data to calibrate the USGS 1DTempPro model to estimate infiltration; and d) ring-infiltrometer measurements to estimate infiltration and hydraulic conductivity of riverbed, overbank and alternate channel alluvium." (ISW Report Executive Summary, PDF p7)
records.notes: Report's own list letters run a)-d) with 'd)' used twice; transcribed verbatim. Quantified results incl. 'On average, losses were 11 cfs/rm from Chualar to the Downstream Bend 1 gaging station, then lowering to 3.4 cfs/rm... and then to 1.0 cfs/rm from Bend 2 to Spreckels' (PDF p30).

records.subsection: Is the concern of differing depletion at varying aquifer depths recognized?
records.finding: The depth question resolves into a definitional one with real accounting consequences. All pumping is below the Salinas Valley Aquitard; all interconnection is above it. The interconnected zone is excluded from principal-aquifer status because nobody pumps it, and DWR accepted that definition.
records.direct_quote: "The Salinas Valley Aquitard extends across much of the Subbasin and inhibits hydraulic connection between the stream and the underlying principal aquifers where groundwater pumping occurs." (Amendment 1 5.6.2, PDF p191)
records.notes: DWR quoted in Periodic Evaluation 1.1.2 (PDF p21): 'Department staff do not believe the SVBGSA erred in its identification of principal aquifers' and 'the SVBGSA did not act unreasonably when defining principal aquifers.' records.subsection: How is water savings calculated?
records.finding: BEST LAND-USE-CHANGE WATER ACCOUNTING IN THE THREE-BASIN CORPUS. The arundo eradication programme publishes a per-acre ET-difference conversion factor with numeric uncertainty, cited to a named study, and explicitly corrected for the vegetation that regrows after treatment.
records.direct_quote: "The study calculates the approximate water savings via a reduction in consumptive use of 21.1 (+/- 3.0) inches or 1.76 (+/- 0.25) feet of water per year over the treated area based on the average difference in ET between untreated arundo and herbaceous vegetation." (Periodic Evaluation 3.3.1, PDF p96)
records.notes: Source study Zefferman and Barker 2024, not on disk. Merced CAUGHT the replacement-vegetation problem post hoc (residual orchard trees); Salinas Valley CORRECTS for it ex ante inside the factor. Two defensible solutions to the same problem - better synthesis material than ranking. | Also touches 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice.

records.subsection: Once a parcel stops pumping, does its paper entitlement to pump get freed up?
records.finding: DESIGN INSIGHT FOR DWR. Acquisition is the only one of the three basins' instruments that is robust to the absence of an allocation system. Merced's and East Turlock's designs both presuppose a functioning entitlement ledger; buying the land removes the pumper rather than regulating them.
records.direct_quote: "The 2020 GSP proposed a Water Charges Framework for the Salinas Valley. Amendment 1 widens the management action to Demand Planning to include other types of demand planning. It separates demand planning from the funding mechanism, so as to not preclude options. Demand planning includes, but is not limited to, pumping allocations, pumping controls, and pumping reductions." (Periodic Evaluation Table 3-1, PDF p91; verified column-aware)
records.notes: STATE THE TRADE-OFF, DO NOT TAKE A SIDE: acquisition is permanent and needs no compliance monitoring, but is capital-intensive, slow (completion 2027, six years after MLRP launch), reaches only willing sellers of marginal land, and - because the GSA does not hold the grant - produces no entry in any SGMA accounting system.

records.subsection: How are those co-benefits tracked and quantified?
records.finding: BEST ECOLOGICAL ACCOUNTING IN THE PROJECT. A per-GDE continuous statistical threshold derived from a regression of vegetation greenness on depth to groundwater, computed only where the relationship is statistically significant, automated in R, and recomputable annually from two public datasets. Merced scores ecological co-benefits by application-stage checkbox; East Turlock uses an optional ordinal visual protocol.
records.direct_quote: "ZDTG threshold = (ZNDVI threshold (i.e. -1) - linear model intercept)/ linear model slope" (GDE report, PDF p19). A GDE is classified of concern for a year if both ZNDVI <= -1 and ZDTG >= ZNDVI.
records.notes: Method follows Rhode et al. (2024), Nature Water. Inputs: Landsat NDVI via TNC GDE Pulse and MCWRA's existing annual groundwater elevations. Only ecological accounting in the project that a platform could run.

records.notes: Reassessment is scheduled to the SGMA cycle: 'It is recommended that this reassessment aligns with the 5-year Periodic Evaluations required by SGMA.' Results for the 180/400: GDEs of concern present in 2015, 2021, 2022 and 2023; none in 2019, 2020 or 2024.

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?
records.finding: The best ecological accounting in the project is connected to nothing. The GDE programme is not adopted, is tied to no sustainable management criterion, and measures the consequence of groundwater depth rather than the consequence of repurposing. The GDE-of-concern years and the sole ISW undesirable-result year overlap and are reconciled nowhere.

records.notes: As an MLRP co-benefit instrument it would need to be run on repurposed parcels against a counterfactual; nothing on disk proposes that. Pair with ISW notes flag 8.

records.finding: AND THE SEAT IS STRUCTURALLY SUBORDINATED ON THE TWO DECISIONS THAT CONSTITUTE DEMAND MANAGEMENT. A 'super majority plus' vote - eight of eleven directors INCLUDING three of the four agricultural representatives - is required to impose fees or to limit well extractions. The DAC, Environmental and Public directors cannot form part of any coalition that adopts a pumping limit over agricultural objection.
records.direct_quote: "A super majority plus requires an affirmative vote by eight of the eleven Board members, including an affirmative vote by three of the four agricultural representatives." (2020 GSP 2.2.1, GSP p. 2-7 / PDF p51). The enumerated items requiring it: "Decisions to impose fees not requiring a vote of the electorate or property owners"; "Proposals to submit to the electorate or property owners (as required by law) decisions to impose fees or taxes"; "Limitations on well extractions (pumping limits)".
records.notes: Same handling class as the Merced leakage architecture finding (Open Question #22): state the structure, never allege the cause. The JPA definition at Appendix 2A PDF p452 words it as 'three of the Agricultural Directors'; the four-seat denominator comes from the body text and the Board roster. 'Super Majority' returns 0 hits in the 2025 Periodic Evaluation - the structure is not revisited.

records.subsection: How are GSAs / subbasins engaging with the broader community?
records.finding: BEST ANSWER TO THE ENGAGEMENT-METHODOLOGY QUESTION IN THE PROJECT, and it is community-authored. Four named conditions: accessibility, self-efficacy, time commitment/logistics, and relevance. Condition (2) states that participation must make a difference to the outcome - precisely what the Super Majority Plus rule constrains for the DAC, environmental and public directors.
records.direct_quote: "(1) Accessibility - information is accessible, in a language and with sufficient background so that all present can understand what is presented (2) Self-efficacy - community member participation makes a difference in the outcome of this plan and groundwater management (3) Time commitment / logistics - meetings are held in familiar locations, close enough to where community members live or work, and at a time when most are available (4) Relevance - the meeting and information is important enough and relevant for community members to prioritize" (CWC comment letter, 2020 GSP Appendix 11G, PDF p1438) [OCR]
records.notes: THE COMMUNITY'S OWN FRAMEWORK NAMES THE FAILURE MODE THE GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE PRODUCES. Connection available from two verified passages, no speculation required.

records.subsection: Monitoring architecture — tiered instruments
records.finding: ETSGSA's MLRP monitoring is built as a three-tier architecture, which is why a reviewer looking for a single 'regional monitoring plan' in Turlock would report an absence and be wrong. Tier 1 is the Implementation Monitoring Plan (phases, frequencies, roles, file naming, QA, DOC reporting) applying to all MLRP projects regardless of practice; Tier 2 is five practice-specific Implementation Standards (Rewilding, Vegetated Cover, Constructed Basins, Stormwater Ponds, General Earthwork) each adding requirements on top; Tier 3 is a per-project instrument selecting which add-ons apply.

records.subsection: Monitoring is landowner self-reported
records.finding: All on-site MLRP monitoring in East Turlock is performed and submitted by the landowner; ETSGSA's own role is receipt, data checks and aggregation for Department of Conservation reporting, not independent field measurement. The agency names the landowner as 'Project Lead Monitor'. There is no independent agency verification step in the monitoring chain - which is what makes the credit-contingent measurement pattern (row 135) consequential: where no credit is sought, the entire evidentiary record is landowner-produced photographs and short forms.

records.subsection: Practice standard spans MLRP and non-MLRP
records.finding: The Vegetated Cover Implementation Standard applies across MLRP and non-MLRP land repurposing alike - to Self-Directed Fallowing and to the Incentivized Fallowing Program (IFP) as well as to MLRP Fallowing. A single technical standard therefore governs practice on land that is inside the grant programme and land that is entirely outside it, which is a transferability point worth surfacing for DWR: the standard does not depend on MLRP grant funding to operate.

records.subsection: Template reuse across practice standards
records.finding: The Stormwater Ponds Implementation Standard internally labels two of its own sections as applying to 'Rewilding Projects' - apparent template reuse across the five practice documents. Its Monitoring section opens 'The following minimum monitoring Requirements shall apply to Rewilding Projects', and its Site Assessment section reads 'Site assessment for Rewilding Projects may vary from project to project'. The document's own title line also splices the two practices ('Implementation Standards and Management Practices for Stormwater Ponds for Rewilding'). Flagged per the Uncertainty Escalation Protocol rather than resolved: it cannot be determined from the documents whether the Rewilding label is a drafting artifact or a deliberate scoping statement, and the credit-contingent monitoring bullets quoted in row 135 sit underneath that heading.

records.subsection: Compliance loop — annual application of the proxy
records.finding: TWO LINKED FACTS IN ONE ROW (see Notes). (i) The WY 2025 Annual Report carries an ISW undesirable-result determination past the Periodic Evaluation's own evaluation window, giving a second independent year of the elevation proxy actually being applied - one exceedance year (WY 2022) and one clean year (WY 2025) across two documents, consistent with an annually-applied criterion rather than a one-off. (ii) But the same document makes an inferential pumping-attribution claim the proxy is not built to support, and it points the opposite way from the WY 2022 determination, which was attributed to reservoir operations rather than pumping - with no stated method distinguishing the two readings. This is the first place in the three-basin corpus where a document attributes a year-over-year proxy change to pumping in narrative prose.
records.direct_quote: "Table 4-9 shows that there was no exceedances of the ISW minimum threshold; therefore, an ISW undesirable result does not exist." (p. 103 [AR PDF 110]). And: "Shallow groundwater elevations declined minimally in the other RMS well (16S/05E-31P02), which could indicate that due to pumping, more depletion of ISW occurred in WY 2025 than in WY 2024." (p. 61 [AR PDF 68])

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.subsection: Domestic well protection — DAC-differential standard
records.finding: No differential protection standard exists for domestic wells in DACs versus elsewhere - in either direction. The tiered well permit review applies uniformly basin-wide with no DAC-specific provision, weighting, or priority, and no minimum threshold anywhere in the GSP is set by reference to DAC status or domestic-well vulnerability.
records.direct_quote: The flowchart's screening criteria are hydrologic and dimensional only: wells pumping '>2 AFY', and within the Focus Area those 'greater than 100 gpm or have a well casing diameter greater than 6-inches'. No DAC or equity criterion appears at any tier.
records.notes: Typical domestic wells fall BELOW these thresholds, so the review screens larger neighbours rather than regulating domestic wells - protective in effect, but not DAC-differentiated. See row 306.

records.subsection: Model class and typology
records.finding: NUMERICAL, and the clearest numerical case in the study. The YSGA Model is a linked surface water-groundwater model coupling WEAP (rainfall-runoff, reservoir operation, demand allocation) to MODFLOW (finite-difference groundwater flow), with the MODFLOW component inheriting inputs, aquifer parameters, boundary conditions and aquifer representation from an earlier Yolo County IWFM. Monthly time step, WY1971-2018, spatial domain extending beyond the subbasin to Clear Lake and Indian Valley Reservoir.
records.direct_quote: "The YSGA model is a linked surface water-groundwater model developed using Water Evaluation and Planning (WEAP) and USGS' modular finite-difference flow model (MODFLOW)."
records.notes: GSP PDF p245 (internal 2-149). Contrast Merced's analytical depletion-factor approach. Critically, model sophistication does NOT translate into threshold-setting - see row 330.

records.subsection: Undesirable result threshold — form of the value
records.finding: Yolo's ISW minimum thresholds are groundwater ELEVATIONS at representative monitoring wells plus a recurrence rule - not depletion volumes. Five ISW Management Zones each carry a different methodology: Lower Cache Creek uses a 1-in-7-year spring recurrence rule; Upper Cache Creek, Putah Creek and Lower Sacramento River use the period-of-record minimum elevation exceeded in 2 consecutive years; Upper Sacramento River uses that minimum plus 20% of the historic max-min range, in 2 consecutive years.
records.direct_quote: "The Minimum Threshold for depletion of interconnected surface water is the recurrence of the spring (March-May) average measurement for 1975 to present in at least one spring in every seven (7) years."
records.notes: GSP PDF p302 (internal 3-24). Zone-specific methodologies within a single indicator is unusual and worth surfacing.

records.subsection: Undesirable result definition — spatial trigger
records.finding: The undesirable result requires exceedance in over 50% of ISW representative monitoring wells in TWO OR MORE ISW management areas in the same reporting year. A single zone in exceedance is designated an 'undesirable result watch area' but is explicitly not an undesirable result. DWR has since issued a corrective action requiring YSGA to justify precisely this two-zone bar.
records.direct_quote: "An undesirable result occurs when the Minimum Threshold is exceeded in over 50 percent of the interconnected surface water representative monitoring wells in two (2) or more interconnected surface water MAs in the same reporting year."
records.notes: GSP PDF p301. DWR corrective action 4a asks YSGA to explain 'how local exceedances within just one management area are not considered an undesirable result' - see row 338.

records.subsection: Threshold relaxed for a non-resource reason
records.finding: A rare, explicit, documented instance of a minimum threshold set BELOW historical conditions for a reason unrelated to the resource condition being protected. The Upper Sacramento River zone threshold is deliberately relaxed to accommodate anticipated reductions in surface water deliveries under State Water Board Voluntary Agreements, which are expected to increase local groundwater reliance.
records.direct_quote: "The minimum thresholds for the North Yolo MA are set lower than historical conditions recognizing that water districts, such as RD 108, in this area may experience reductions in surface water deliveries from the Sacramento River as potential Voluntary Agreements with the State Water Board are implemented."
records.notes: GSP PDF p304 (internal 3-25). A supply-policy accommodation written into an environmental threshold. Highly relevant to the DWR recommendations on threshold-setting discipline.

records.subsection: Monitoring network design rule
records.finding: 17 near-stream shallow RMWs across five ISW Management Zones, measured semi-annually (spring and fall). Selection criteria are explicit and EDF-2018-derived: adequate period of record; screened in or near the shallow aquifer; representative of the gradient between stream and centre of pumping; and historical water-level variation greater than 10 ft, ideally 50 ft or more, so that readings are not dominated by river stage. Spatial density target is one well every 4 to 6 miles of stream.
records.direct_quote: "Representative monitoring wells were selected to produce a good spatial distribution along major interconnected surface water bodies, ideally one well for every 4 to 6 miles along the stream (see: Addressing Regional Surface Water Depletions in California, EDF 2018)."
records.notes: GSP PDF p333 (internal 4-23) and p328 (internal 4-22). A replicable, citable design rule - unusual in this document class.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.subsection: Per-well attribution (cumulative pumping problem)
records.finding: No per-well attribution of ISW depletion exists anywhere in the Yolo corpus, and the cumulative pumping problem is not named, discussed, or accounted for. This is structural rather than an oversight: the proxy attributes depletion to aggregate near-stream groundwater elevation within a management zone, so the accounting has no unit of analysis smaller than an ISW Management Zone and no mechanism that could produce a per-well number.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary searches across the full 1,049-page GSP for 'cumulative effect|cumulative impact|cumulative pumping|individual well.*impact|per-well|well-by-well|attribut*' return no ISW-related hits. Positive controls confirm the search works: the same 'attribut*' search returns "subsidence can be attributed to other tectonic activities, and not solely groundwater extractions" and "Salinity in Yolo Subbasin can be attributed to a variety of land use factors". The vocabulary of attribution exists in this GSP; it is never applied to ISW.
records.notes: Positive controls at GSP PDF p295. DWR corrective action 4e asks YSGA to identify even the USERS affected by pumping-induced depletion, let alone the pumps responsible.

records.finding: The concern is recognised in monitoring design but foreclosed at the source by missing data. records.subsection: Aquifer depth differentiation — stated assumption
records.finding: The reconciliation across depths is an explicit stated assumption: shallow and intermediate zones are treated as hydraulically continuous because no confining layer has been observed between them - justified by absence of contrary evidence rather than positive evidence. RMW selection is depth-controlled, preferring wells shallower than 220 ft with the deepest selected well at 350 ft. Layering is also non-uniform: three layers subbasin-wide but a five-layer representation for Capay Valley inherited from RMC's 2016 IGSM.
records.direct_quote: "Screened within, or close to, the shallow aquifer as defined in the hydrogeologic conceptual model. Wells shallower than 220 feet were preferred, with the deepest selected well drilled to a depth of 350 feet. Water levels at wells within the top portion of the intermediate zone are still considered to affect surface water bodies because both the shallow and intermediate zones are largely alluvial and there is no evidence showing a confining layer between the two zones."
records.notes: GSP PDF p328 (internal 4-22); Capay 5-layer at PDF p107 (internal 2-11). A clearly stated and clearly justified simplifying assumption - good practice on communication even where the evidence base is thin.

records.finding: Uncertainty is communicated as a qualitative narrative buried in a 162-page technical appendix, not as a property of the published numbers. records.subsection: Compliance loop — deliberately severed
records.finding: Uniquely among the four basins, the model-to-threshold link is held open DELIBERATELY and with a stated reason. YSGA builds a numerical WEAP/MODFLOW model, obtains depletion-relevant outputs from it, and then declines to set thresholds on them because it judges the model too uncertain. The loop runs: model -> (severed) -> elevation proxy thresholds -> annual pass/fail count -> no management action triggered in the period of record.
records.direct_quote: "The YSGA's integrated WEAP/MODFLOW model (YSGA Model) provides estimates of the quantity and timing of groundwater-surface water exchange; however, the model contains uncertainties such that setting thresholds based around model outputs is not appropriate."
records.notes: GSP PDF p300 (internal 3-22). The most important single ISW quote in the Yolo corpus for the DWR recommendations: a sophisticated model that its own owner will not threshold on.

records.subsection: Well permitting — stream proximity criterion
records.finding: The only place ISW enters a binding decision, and it is prospective and qualitative rather than accounting-based. The YSGA Tiered Well Permit Review inserts 'anticipated impacts on nearby interconnected surface waters' as one of five Tier 1 concerns; a flagged application escalates to Tier 2 requiring a hydrogeologist report from a California-licensed PG or CHG; and YSGA withholds written verification where the preponderance of evidence shows the well would exceed GSP minimum thresholds. Yolo County makes the final determination, and the flowchart is marked DRAFT.
records.direct_quote: "The YSGA will not issue written verification where, based on that record, the preponderance of the evidence shows that the proposed well: (a) Will result in an exceedance of the Minimum Thresholds identified in the GSP, or (b) Will interfere with the production and functioning of existing nearby wells, or (c) Will cause subsidence that would adversely impact or damage nearby critical infrastructure."
records.notes: Converts ISW from a monitored condition into a permit criterion - closing model-to-decision in the FORWARD direction while measuring and crediting nothing. Note it is DRAFT and the County holds final say.

records.subsection: Well permitting — entity holding the authority
records.finding: The binding permitting authority is Yolo County's, not the GSA's. The County's 2024 Urgency Ordinance conditions agricultural well permits in unincorporated Yolo County on GSP consistency, administered through Yolo County Environmental Health. YSGA supplies the verification; the County issues or denies the permit. Entity attribution matters: this is a County instrument acting on a GSA determination.
records.direct_quote: "While the YSGA is responsible for the sustainability of the groundwater basin, the County's Division of Environmental Health (also known as 'Yolo County Environmental Health' or 'YCEH') is the local enforcement agency responsible for issuing permits for groundwater wells in the County, including new wells, alterations to existing wells, and replacement wells."
records.notes: The GSA's only hard lever runs through a Member's own regulatory authority - a governance pattern worth surfacing for single-GSA JPA basins generally.

records.subsection: Published data-certainty ratings

records.subsection: Co-benefit accounting schema
records.finding: Appendix J's Expected Benefits schema forecloses co-benefit accounting: it recognises exactly four benefit types, all hydrological - Water Supply Augmentation and Water Demand Reduction (Primary), Water Quality Improvement and Water Management Flexibility/Efficiency (Secondary). There is no column for habitat, ecosystem, DAC, economic, recreational, heat or dust benefit. Habitat projects are therefore recorded by what they do for water: P 58, the oak woodland/riparian/chaparral restoration, is marked only under Water Quality Improvement.

P 58 bullet appears in Water Quality Improvement only (ink ratio 0.0106 vs 0.0000 adjacent).
records.notes: Any Pass 2 claim that Yolo tracks co-benefits must be resisted - the data structure makes it impossible. GSP prose recognises ecological value ('can improve the hydrological and ecological function of these areas') with no metric, baseline, threshold, or unit.

records.subsection: Monitoring protocol for repurposing
records.finding: No monitoring requirements exist for water savings or co-benefits of land repurposing, because no programme exists to impose them. There is no enrolment agreement, no implementation standards, no incentive-payment procedure, no monitoring plan and no verification protocol for any repurposing-type activity. East Turlock has ten standalone MLRP programme instruments; Yolo has none.
records.direct_quote: The Yolo basin folder contains only the GSP, its appendices, the Annual Report, the JPA, a Board orientation packet, a County well ordinance and a draft flowchart. No programme instrument of any kind exists.

records.subsection: Dust / PM mitigation measurement
records.finding: Dust savings are not quantified, accounted for, or mentioned by YSGA. The 'loud but invisible' pattern with an unusually clean signature: every dust, PM10 and air-quality hit in the GSP sits inside a PUBLIC COMMENT letter, not YSGA text, and YSGA's own text contains zero occurrences. The topic enters the record from the public and exits without a response.

records.notes: GSP PDF p497. Fourth basin, fourth confirmation that no basin in this study has a field-scale dust accounting method - but Yolo is the first where the public raises it and the GSA does not take it up.

records.subsection: Machine-readability of the PMA status register
records.finding: GSP Appendix J - 89 rows by 21 columns of funding, cost, implementer, status and DAC data in the adopted GSP of a high-priority basin - is completely unreadable by any text extraction tool. All four embedded fonts carry no ToUnicode map (pdffonts uni:no), so pdftotext, pdftohtml and pdfminer each return only stray page numbers on every page. records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.subsection: Cumulative pumping problem
records.finding: The cumulative pumping problem is explicitly recognised — and the GSA's response is to define it out of the monitoring network rather than to build an attribution method. Wells whose capture cannot be disentangled are the wells excluded from the ISW network; the depletion they cause is not attributed elsewhere.
records.direct_quote: "Wells deeper than 200 feet and farther than five miles from interconnected streams were excluded because pumping at greater depths or distances was assumed to cause capture from multiple sources (e.g., recharge zones, springs, ponded water, and other wells), which cannot be resolved with existing data and models"
records.notes: GSP PDF 355 (printed 5-27). Clearest statement of the cumulative-pumping problem found in any basin so far; absence of a method for a problem the GSA names is a sharper finding than a silent absence.

records.subsection: Why Colusa is not a grantee
records.finding: Appendix 7A positions Colusa outside MLRP explicitly and gives the reason: the programme targets Critically Overdrafted subbasins, and Colusa is high-priority but not critically overdrafted. This is a cleaner account of non-grantee status than Yolo's documents offered.
records.direct_quote: "While the program would primarily be targeted to the Critically Overdrafted Subbasins, potential multi-benefit recharge projects included in the Colusa Subbasin GSP (see Chapter 6) may be eligible under this or similar programs."

records.subsection: Dust
records.finding: (a) NOT MENTIONED. Dust is not considered in any repurposing, recharge or land-use project in the Colusa Subbasin, therefore not measured and not accounted for. A dust accounting module in GAP would have no Colusa data to ingest.

records.subsection: Crediting mechanism or enrolment process
records.finding: No crediting mechanism, enrolment process, application or verification protocol exists for any land repurposing activity. records.subsection: Caveat — GEEEO/model consistency asserted, not shown
records.finding: The technical memorandum asserts a comparison it does not provide. The GSP's water budgets came from the C2VSimFG-Colusa model; the WY2025 Annual Report's extraction volumes come from GEEEO, a residual method. The memo states the two were compared 'to ensure consistency' and publishes no comparison table, scatter, percentage difference or reconciliation anywhere in the document set. The finding is the claim itself: a comparison stated as performed, with its result unpublished. Extraction in GEEEO is derived as a residual, so any error in ET or surface supply lands on the extraction figure — the basin is managed against one set of numbers and reported against another, with the relationship undisclosed.
records.direct_quote: "key inputs and results from the GEEEO process have been compared with those of the GSP groundwater model to ensure consistency in the water use analyses"
records.notes: AR App D section 1, PDF 153 (printed 147). SCOPE DECISION 2026-09-10 (Jackson): note the asserted-but-unprovided comparison as a finding in its own right; do NOT request the underlying analysis. Nothing outstanding on this item.

records.subsection: Model class and typology
records.finding: One shared numerical model: MODFLOW-OWHM V2, four layers (Upper Aquifer, Corcoran Clay aquitard, two Lower Aquifer layers), 500-ft grid, monthly stress periods, historical WY1999-2022 and predictive WY2023-2072. records.direct_quote: "In 2023 and 2024, M&A, with contributions from INTERA (representing the East Kaweah GSA) and Thomas Harder & Co. (representing the Greater Kaweah GSA), implemented temporal updates and structural enhancements to the Model to support GSP amendments. Major updates included the development of the Farm Process (FMP4) and Streamflow Routing (SFR) packages" (Modeling Report Sec 2, GKGSA GSP PDF 2472-2473)

records.subsection: Model capability vs model use for ISW
records.finding: The basin has a stream-routing package inside a numerical groundwater model and states on the page that it was added for FUTURE use. The ISW analysis therefore does not run on the numerical model at all.
records.direct_quote: "The implementation of the SFR package enhanced the Model's capability to simulate inflows, diversions, and interactions within natural channels, thereby refining the estimation of surface water seepage and its connections to groundwater along the main river systems for potential future applications." records.subsection: Measurement method - analytical depletion model
records.finding: Because the numerical model cannot do ISW, depletion is estimated with an ANALYTICAL stream-depletion function - Hunt (1999, 2005) - run stochastically over a range of streambed and aquifer properties for well distances 50-2,000 ft over a six-month pumping period. Kaweah is the first basin in this study to run an analytical depletion model at all. The TM states the tool's limits on the same page.
records.direct_quote: "The analytical model relies on simplifying assumptions (for example, constant connectivity and stage in River) which makes it unsuitable to estimate long-term depletions with dynamic flow conditions and interconnectedness between the surface water and groundwater systems." (ISW TM Sec 3.2, GKGSA GSP PDF 2761)

records.subsection: Threshold scope - what the MT does and does not oblige
records.finding: The MT is explicitly not a flow-maintenance obligation. It applies only where DEPLETIONS drive flows below WY 2022 levels; hydrologic and other anthropogenic causes are carved out. records.subsection: Depletion derivation - the 5% factor
records.finding: The 5% factor is the MOST CONSERVATIVE end of the modelled range applied as an AVERAGE, because well locations are unknown. Hunt analytical modelling gave 2% (well 2,000 ft away) to 5% (well 50 ft away) of pumped volume derived from the stream over six months at 90% likelihood; the 50-ft value was adopted basin-reach-wide.
records.direct_quote: "The results show that for this portion of the Kaweah River, 2% (for a well 2,000 ft away) to 5% (for a well 50 ft away) of the pumped volume could be derived from the stream over the six-month pumping period with a 90% likelihood. records.notes: The stated direction of bias is conservative (over-estimating depletion). This is the clearest worked example in the study of an accounting parameter chosen because the underlying data does not exist.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.subsection: Cumulative pumping problem
records.finding: STRONGER ABSENCE THAN COLUSA'S. Colusa at least names capture and says it cannot be resolved with existing data and models. Kaweah's ISW TM does not use the words cumulative, superposition or capture in the depletion analysis at all. A Hunt analytical solution for a single well at a single distance is applied as a flat percentage against aggregate pumping - superposition by assumption, with no check that the linear-superposition conditions hold and no treatment of the lagged accumulating component.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary search of the ISW Technical Memorandum (GKGSA GSP PDF 2736-2783) returns zero occurrences of the terms cumulative, superposition and capture in the depletion analysis. Positive controls pass: depletion 100+, pumping 60+, analytical 12. The only forward statement is that long-term transient depletion “will be conducted using the refined groundwater model” (Sec 3.2, PDF 2761).

records.subsection: Aquifer depth differentiation - recognition
records.finding: Depth differentiation is recognised structurally and better than in most basins here. The Corcoran Clay divides the system into Upper and Lower Aquifers; the model represents it as an explicit aquitard with two Lower Aquifer layers beneath, the split justified by AEM resistivity zoning from a Stanford/USGS survey. Nearly every SMC in the basin is set separately for Upper and Lower Aquifers, and per-well hydrographs are tagged by aquifer (Single / Upper / Lower).
records.direct_quote: "Stanford also updated the Model from a 3-layer to a 4-layer structure that included the Upper Aquifer, Corcoran Clay as an aquitard, and 2 lower aquifer layers." (Modeling Report Sec 2, GKGSA GSP PDF 2472)

records.subsection: Aquifer depth differentiation - ISW reconciliation
records.finding: The ISW monitoring network is confined to the Upper Aquifer by its own selection test, and NO vertical reconciliation between Upper and Lower Aquifer pumping and stream depletion is performed anywhere. This matters more here than in a single-aquifer basin: Kaweah's overdraft and subsidence problem is a Lower Aquifer problem, so the aquifer being managed hardest is the one excluded from the ISW analysis.
records.direct_quote: "Is the well drilled in the upper aquifer with the screen at an appropriate depth?" - first of five Shallow Aquifer RMS Well Considerations (EKGSA GSP Sec 4.7.3.1, PDF 301; same text at ISW TM Sec 4.2.1, GKGSA GSP PDF 2771)
records.notes: Subsidence context: "land subsidence results primarily from depressurization and subsequent compaction of clay interbed materials within the Lower Aquifer" (Modeling Report Sec 3.6, GKGSA GSP PDF 2486).

records.subsection: Plan to remedy the gaps
records.finding: An adopted management action with four named phases: MA7 Interconnected Surface Water Data Gap Work Plan, first developed 2022 and revised for the 2024 amendments. Phase 1 filling data gaps and further research; Phase 2 analytical tool development; Phase 3 interconnection analysis and impact attribution analysis; Phase 4 SMC refinement and incorporation into the 5-year GSP update. records.subsection: Scope limitation - no flow objective exists
records.finding: UNIQUE TO KAWEAH AMONG THE FIVE BASINS. The river is fully appropriated under pre-1914 rights administered by the Kaweah and St. Johns River Association, Terminus Dam captures about 95 percent of watershed runoff, and no minimum flow condition or flow objective exists anywhere in the subbasin. The GSAs identify this as the reason a depletion threshold cannot be anchored to an endpoint. Strongest version in the study of an ISW indicator with no measurable endpoint of its own.
records.direct_quote: "no minimum flow conditions or flow objectives have been established in the Subbasin. The Kaweah River System is fully appropriated and highly impacted by factors outside the GSAs control (Kaweah releases, hydrology, diversions, etc)." (ISW TM Sec 1, GKGSA GSP PDF 2742; repeated at Sec 5, PDF 2774)
records.notes: "Without such minimum flow requirements or flow objectives, it is challenging to identify depletions that would lead to significant and unreasonable reductions in flows with corresponding impacts" (ISW TM Sec 3.2, PDF 2757). Compare East Turlock Open Question #108 - externalisation of the ecological endpoint.

records.subsection: Uncertainty - propagation to the criterion
records.finding: None of the three published uncertainty statements is propagated to the ISW criterion. The model is calibrated to RMSE 32.2 ft with mean residuals within plus or minus 25 ft; the groundwater-level MTs in the ISW area are set at Fall 2022 water levels plus 1 to 2 additional feet of decline; and the document set never puts the two numbers side by side. The Colusa finding in a far more extreme form.
records.direct_quote: "The interim SMC established for ISW are based on groundwater conditions in 2022. This is consistent with the SMC established for groundwater levels and groundwater storage in this portion of the Subbasin as the MTs in the easternmost portions of the Subbasin (where potential ISW are) were set to Fall 2022 groundwater levels (+1 to 2 additional feet of decline on the westernmost portion of the ISW, where the existing evaluation suggests the stream reaches are likely disconnected)." (ISW TM Sec 3.5, GKGSA GSP PDF 2766)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-4): both figures verified verbatim, but the COMPARISON is the extractor's inference, not the document's, and the quantities are not strictly commensurable - a basin-wide calibration statistic is not a local prediction error, and the ISW MT is a flow criterion the level criterion is merely declared consistent with. State as "the level criterion the ISW criterion is declared consistent with sits inside the model's calibration error."

records.subsection: Uncertainty - stochastic confidence on the depletion estimate
records.finding: The analytical depletion estimate carries an explicit confidence statement over multiple stochastic realisations of streambed and aquifer properties - 2% to 5% of pumped volume with a 90% likelihood. Kaweah and Colusa are the only basins in this study that attach a stated confidence level to a depletion-relevant number, and Kaweah is the only one that does it stochastically.
records.direct_quote: "Figure 3-31 shows the likelihood (for multiple stochastic realizations of the streambed and aquifer properties) of the percentage of pumped water derived from the stream for a range of distances (from 50 ft to 2,000 ft) over a six-month pumping period." (ISW TM Sec 3.2, GKGSA GSP PDF 2761)
records.notes: The confidence statement is then discarded when the 5% endpoint is adopted as a point estimate - see the fivepct row.

records.subsection: Uncertainty - dedicated section on ISW designation confidence

records.subsection: Stream-aquifer exchange inside the binding ledger - credit side
records.finding: HEADLINE. Stream seepage is a named component of the quantity landowners are ALLOCATED. GKGSA's binding Native Sustainable Yield definition includes streambed percolation within the natural tributaries of the Kaweah River, cross-referenced to the Coordination Agreement's Water Accounting Framework.

(GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R Sec 3.02(a)(A), PDF 12)
records.notes: State as architecture, not as an allegation - there is no evidence this has been exploited and no reporting by which it could be detected. Pairs with Merced Open Questions #31 and #46.

records.subsection: Stream-aquifer exchange inside the binding ledger - credit side
records.finding: The Water Accounting Framework confirms the same at basin level. Table 3-1 'Groundwater Inflow Components' lists 'Streambed percolation (natural channels) from Kaweah River watershed sources' as a NATIVE inflow - inflows which all well owners have access to on a pro-rata basis - and 'Streambed percolation from imported sources' as FOREIGN. Stream-aquifer exchange is therefore inside the allocation arithmetic as a credit at both GSA and subbasin level.
records.direct_quote: TABLE TRANSCRIPTION, not a continuous span. Coordination Agreement App 3, Table 3-1 "Groundwater Inflow Components" (PDF 432) [OCR]. Native row header: "Native – Inflows which all well owners have access to on a pro-rata basis". Native components listed: "Percolation from rainfall"; "Streambed percolation (natural channels) from Kaweah River watershed sources"; "Agricultural land irrigation returns from pumped groundwater"; "Mountain front recharge". Foreign components include "Streambed percolation from imported sources".
records.notes: [OCR] provenance - the Water Accounting Framework text layer drops "ti" from every word. Single-source: the same appendix appears inside all three GSPs but with identical corruption, so those copies are not independent verification.

records.subsection: Stream-aquifer exchange inside the binding ledger - debit side
records.finding: Both rulebooks exclude the riparian corridor from the consumptive-use debit. So the stream-aquifer interface is inside the binding accounting system in exactly two ways and both run in the pumper's favour: river seepage is credited as native yield that can be allocated and pumped, and riparian evapotranspiration inside a parcel is exempted from the debit. Depletion of the same interface is debited nowhere.
records.direct_quote: "If a watercourse, including canals, ditches, or riparian areas, is located within the boundaries of a parcel of Eligible Land, the area of that watercourse will not be included in the evaluation of any Consumptive Use." (EKGSA R&R Sec 6.04, PDF 6; materially identical at GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R, PDF 10)
records.notes: Direct parallel to Merced Open Question #46 (riparian ET exempted, 150-ft riparian standard disconnected from the ISW indicator). Kaweah is the first basin where the CREDIT side is explicitly named in binding rule text.

records.subsection: Accounting framework currency
records.finding: The Water Accounting Framework the two rulebooks run on has not been updated since 2020 - it predates the model rebuild, the AEM survey, the FMP4 and SFR packages and the entire ISW analysis. The Coordination Agreement's Appendix 5 Data Gaps Summary is likewise 2020-vintage inside a November 2024 agreement.
records.direct_quote: "It should be noted that the WAF has not been updated since 2020 because the GSAs’ focus has been on addressing state-identified deficiencies, including an intensive update of the numerical groundwater model in the Kaweah Subbasin that is used to establish an updated water budget" [OCR] (Coordination Agreement App 3, PDF 431)
records.notes: The same appendix says updating it "is a high priority for the GSAs to assist with WY 2026 allocations anticipated to be set in July 2025". App 5 states it "represents the gaps that were iden fied at the me of 2020 GSP prepara on" [OCR] (PDF 438).

records.subsection: Inter-GSA coordination on ISW
records.finding: ISW is absent from the instrument that coordinates the three GSAs. The Coordination Agreement's 18-page body mentions interconnected surface water exactly once, in the recital listing the six sustainability indicators. No ISW-specific coordination provision, no allocation of ISW responsibility between EKGSA and GKGSA, and no joint depletion accounting - in a basin where potential ISW sits on two rivers that both GSAs border.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary search of the Coordination Agreement body (PDF 1-18): "interconnected" appears once, at PDF 5 - "Sustainability indicators include 1) chronic lowering of groundwater levels, 2) reduction of groundwater storage, 3) seawater intrusion [not applicable], 4) degraded groundwater quality, 5) land subsidence, and 6) depletions of interconnected surface water." The seven appendices are Basin Setting, Monitoring Networks, Water Accounting Framework, Data Management System, Data Gaps, Sustainability Goal and Undesirable Results, and Model Simulation Results.

records.subsection: Entity divergence - ISW presence and monitoring obligation
records.finding: ENTITY-LEVEL DIVERGENCE. MKGSA has no ISW and operates no ISW monitoring network, invoking Sec 354.34(j). EKGSA and GKGSA hold all of the basin's potential ISW, and most of it falls in GKGSA. Never write 'Kaweah monitors ISW at three wells' - that is EKGSA and GKGSA.
records.direct_quote: "In the MKGSA, the connection of surface water and groundwater was disconnected many decades ago. Therefore, a monitoring network and monitoring is not required for the MKGSA." (MKGSA GSP Sec 4.7, PDF 244, printed p.4-66)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-1): the supporting analysis is the subbasin ISW TM's DTW mapping ("DTW in the west are consistently greater than 50 ft, so there is little to no likelihood of ISWs in the western portions of GKGSA and the entire MKGSA area", PDF 2751) - but that TM's own Sec 2.4 says the DTW surface is Spring-2017-based and that designations "are preliminary and may be refined". A monitoring exemption granted on a preliminary designation is not a contradiction, but the two statements sit at different confidence levels and the GSP does not reconcile them.

records.subsection: Regulatory history driving the ISW revision
records.finding: Kaweah is the only basin in this study to have gone to a State Water Board probationary process, and the ISW chapter exists in its current form because of it. DWR Incomplete (Jan 2022) -> DWR Inadequate (Mar 2023) -> SWRCB jurisdiction -> SWRCB Draft Staff Report (May 2024) identifying ISW Deficiencies 1-3 (beneficial uses/users, MT justification, monitoring network) -> 2nd Amended GSPs (Nov 2024) -> SWRCB adequacy determination and release from probation (Dec 2025).
records.direct_quote: "In early December 2025, the SWRCB deemed the updated GSPs adequate for SGMA compliance and returned the Kaweah Subbasin back to DWR and out of probation." (Annual Report Sec 4.1, PDF 29, printed p.4-1)
records.notes: DOCUMENT-SCOPE GAP: the SWRCB May 2024 Draft Staff Report and the December 2025 adequacy determination are NOT on disk. They are the direct regulator critique of exactly the accounting methods this project studies, and are the highest-value missing documents for this basin.
records.source_title: Kaweah Subbasin WY 2025 Annual Monitoring Report (April 2026)

records.subsection: Regulator deficiency finding on the prior threshold
records.finding: The SWRCB's ISW-2 deficiency is the cleanest external statement in the study of what a defensible ISW minimum threshold requires, and Kaweah's response is that it still cannot meet it. The TM's own conclusion says ISW-1 and ISW-2 cannot be fully addressed at this time.
records.direct_quote: "Deficiency ISW-2: The GSPs did not provide sufficient justification for minimum thresholds (the lowest acceptable level) for depletions of interconnected surface water. The MTs established by the GSPs are not supported with best available information, best available science, or a model that quantifies surface water depletion." (SWRCB May 2024 Draft Staff Report, quoted at ISW TM Sec 1, GKGSA GSP PDF 2741)
records.notes: Quoted at second hand - the ISW TM excerpts the SWRCB report, which is not itself on disk. The TM Sec 5 response to ISW-2 is "Established framework to develop MTs based on historical impacts. Evaluated Preliminary MTs based on channel loss, pumping, and depletion estimates" (PDF 2773).

records.subsection: Machine readability of the accounting instrument
records.finding: MACHINE-READABILITY THREAD - highest-consequence instance found in the project, because the affected document is an ACCOUNTING INSTRUMENT rather than a technical appendix. The Water Accounting Framework (Coordination Agreement App 3) and the Data Gaps Summary (App 5) silently drop the letter pair 'ti' from every word containing it. The text extracts, reads as prose and is quotable - so a quote copied from it is silently wrong. Six pages per document, replicated across all three GSPs and the standalone Coordination Agreement (24 page-instances of one 6-page document).
records.direct_quote: Raw pdftotext output, Coordination Agreement PDF 431: "A Water Accoun ng Framework (WAF) was developed by the three Kaweah Subbasin GSAs to direct development of projects and management ac ons and to track beneﬁts accrued by each project and management ac on." The fi ligature survives; the ti pair does not.
records.notes: Second basin instance of the Salinas Valley "fails loudly but invisibly" class (Salinas 2020 GSP PDF 1408-1440; Merced GSP PDF 481-482 dropped capitals). Kaweah also carries three other machine-readability failures - see the ISW notes verification box and tools/kaweah_decode.py.

records.subsection: Block grant - holder and amount
records.finding: HEADLINE. Kaweah holds a $10 million Department of Conservation MLRP block grant - the largest in this study - held by the SUBBASIN directly rather than by one GSA or an outside partner. The only description of the programme anywhere in 12,984 pages of filed documents was written by Self-Help Enterprises in a public comment; the GSAs' response is one sentence of thanks.
records.direct_quote: "The Kaweah Subbasin applied for and received $10 million in MLRP funding. The Department of Conservation's MLRP program aims to support coordinated planning of land repurposing projects that balance groundwater supply and demand." (EKGSA GSP PDF 1941, Comment column; replicated GKGSA PDF 1844, MKGSA PDF 1834)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-1): commenter-authored, GSA-unrebutted. Column-aware extraction (Comment x<430pt, Response x>=430pt) confirms attribution; Commenter cell at PDF 1938 reads "Self-Help Enterprises". Four-way grant comparison: Merced $8.89M/MSGSA; East Turlock $8.89M/Subbasin; Salinas Valley $10M/IRWM; Kaweah $10M/Subbasin. Verify the $10M coincidence with Salinas Valley before the two appear in one sentence - cf. Open Question #66.

records.subsection: Method - false absence risk
records.finding: METHOD FINDING. A word-boundary sweep of all 12,984 pages returns MLRP on 5 pages, land repurpos* on 10, block grant on 0 and Department of Conservation on 2. On those counts Kaweah reads as a non-grantee basin. The programme is real, funded and under way - it simply does not appear in the GSP bodies. Eighth-plus instance of the false-absence family and a NEW SUB-TYPE: the programme is documented only in the public comment record.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary counts across the full 12,984-page Kaweah corpus: "MLRP" 5 pages; "land repurpos" 10 pages; "block grant" 0 pages; "Department of Conservation" 2 pages. Positive controls pass: "fallow" 54 pages, "allocation" 300+ pages, "on-farm recharge" 60 pages, "demand management" 250+ pages.
records.notes: Standing lesson for future basins: read the public comment matrix in full during the MLRP pass, not only during Community. Companion to the Yolo lesson about the Annual Report implementation narrative (row 411).

records.subsection: Programme targets - units
records.finding: The Kaweah MLRP's only published quantities are ACRES, not acre-feet. No water saving, water benefit or groundwater quantity is attached to the programme anywhere in the document set. Compare Merced (25,911 AF five-year commitment vs 4,655 AF measured) and East Turlock (four published demand-reduction figures). Kaweah's MLRP has an acreage target and no water target at all. Also the only appearance of a tribal beneficiary in any MLRP material in this study.
records.direct_quote: "The projects approved through this program will help repurpose an estimated 238 acres of retired irrigation land to recharge basins while also restoring 65+ acres for habitat and community/tribal use." (EKGSA GSP PDF 1942, Comment column)

records.subsection: Co-benefits named at project level
records.finding: Flying Dragon is the best-specified multi-benefit repurposing project in this study on the co-benefit SIDE: a quantified water benefit (1,000 AF recharge), habitat, a recreational benefit delivered as a walking trail, a conservation easement as the durability instrument, and a named DAC (Seville) as intended beneficiary. Delivery mechanism is ACQUISITION, as in Salinas Valley. EKGSA is the only Kaweah GSA to have completed an MLRP land purchase.
records.direct_quote: "Flying Dragon is a multi-benefit land repurposing project. The GSA completed the land purchase process in February. Once constructed, the Flying Dragon Recharge Basin project will provide 1,000 acre-feet of groundwater recharge, an environmental habitat, and recreational benefits with a new recharge basin and walking trail through a conservation easement area." (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report PDF 8)
records.notes: The 1,000 AF is a recharge design yield, not a demand reduction, and none of the four benefits carries a measurement or verification protocol. The one MLRP project described in any detail in this basin is described in a GSA NEWSLETTER, not in a plan.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.subsection: ET product choice and the reason for it
records.finding: Land IQ, basin-wide, and the GSA states openly that it chose satellite ET because metering could not be delivered in time. Third ET product across five basins: Merced OpenET; East Turlock LandIQ + CalETa; Kaweah Land IQ; Colusa GEEEO (OpenET ensemble); Salinas Valley none. The accounting architecture does not depend on the ET vendor - strengthens the platform-agnostic GAP finding.
records.direct_quote: "Due to the inability to implement GSA-wide metering in time to initiate the Emergency Ordinance, the MKGSA contracted with Land IQ to track field-level ET using satellite images and ground sensors for calibration." (MKGSA GSP Sec 6.7.1.2, PDF 390, printed p.6-53)
records.notes: Merced made ET the default with meters elective; MIUGSA meters and uses ET only absent a meter; East Turlock uses ET but exempts MLRP project areas from it by rule. Kaweah adopted ET under time pressure and then built the whole ledger on it.

records.subsection: Verification trigger - fallowing determination
records.finding: The binding rule conditions the fallowing benefit on verification and never says how verification is done. No method, standard, evidence requirement, frequency or responsible party is stated. Contrast East Turlock Phase 2 Sec 4.04, which specifies a quantified three-stage remote-sensing cascade for exactly this determination. Kaweah has the ET infrastructure East Turlock uses and does not write the test down.
records.direct_quote: "Parcels which have received a Tier 1 or Tier 2 Penalty Allocation may fallow lands associated with the allocation. Once verified, the fallowed lands will not be debited for any consumptive use on said lands. All parcels must be maintained to limit the growth of any vegetation. Parcels which have been fallowed during a portion of any water year shall receive a pro rata debit (for example, a parcel which begins fallowing at the beginning of June would still be charged for consumptive use for the period October – May)." (GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R Sec 4.03(e), PDF 17)

records.subsection: Allocation interaction - forfeiture vs retention
records.finding: EKGSA goes further than GKGSA: fallowed land is defined as ET Credit Acreage and EARNS an ET Credit back to the landowner's usage account. Read precisely - it is a measurement-error correction that refunds ET the satellite attributes to land the landowner is not irrigating, NOT a repurposing incentive. But its practical effect is that fallowed acreage in EKGSA is not merely un-debited, it generates a credit.
records.direct_quote: "ET Credit Acreage" means land that, at the time of ET measurement by the Agency, is either (a) Fallowed, (b) is a parcel consisting of five acres or less with less than two of those five acres devoted to agricultural use, or (c) Non-Irrigated Land." (EKGSA Rules and Regulations Sec 1.09, PDF 1)
records.notes: Companion definition, Sec 1.10 PDF 1: "Excess ET" means the amount by which any ET calculated by the Agency for ET Credit Acreage exceeds effective precipitation for the subject ET Credit Acreage as a result of any limitations in ET calculation. Do NOT present as an incentive payment in Pass 2.

records.subsection: Transfer regime - geometry and limits
records.finding: The most fully specified transfer regime in the study. Native Sustainable Yield carries over on a five-year rolling basis and transfers within GKGSA on a written form; Tier 1 and Tier 2 transfers are capped at three zones from the transferor's location; out-of-GSA use is permitted under four conditions (common ownership, within the Kaweah Subbasin, reciprocal GSA, written, both GSAs informed); a transferee may not re-transfer; Tier 3 cannot be carried over or transferred at all; and every transfer is subject to clawback keyed to undesirable results.

(GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R, PDF 14-15; parallel provision for Tier 1/2 at PDF 17)

records.subsection: Anti-leakage haircut - distance-graded
records.finding: BEST ANTI-LEAKAGE GEOMETRY IN THE STUDY. A leave-behind that is both distance-graded and tier-graded: Tier 1 pays 20% within zone, 30% to an adjacent zone, 40% at two zones, 70% at three zones; Tier 2 pays 40/50/60/90%. Merced's Leave-Behind is a flat 10% hydrologic haircut; MIUGSA's Pooling Zones are directional but unexplained; East Turlock never adopted transfers; Colusa wrote the principle with no allocation to apply it to. Kaweah prices distance, and prices the more speculative tier more heavily at every distance.
records.direct_quote: TABLE TRANSCRIPTION, not a continuous span. GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R PDF 16, table keyed to Exhibit C. Column headers are stacked across several wrapped lines and are reconstructed here without quotation marks because no continuous span exists: [Transfer within Zone] | [Immediate adjacent Zone from Transferor Place of Use Allocation] | [Total distance of two zones from Transferor Place of Use Allocation (e.g., Zone 35 to 32)] | [Total distance of three zones from Transferor Place of Use Allocation (e.g., Zone 35 to 11)]. Row values — Tier 1: 20% / 30% / 40% / 70%. Tier 2: 40% / 50% / 60% / 90%. Gating condition, verified as a continuous span on the same page: "The place of use is no further than three zones from where the transferor’s location of allocation".
records.notes: NUMERIC COMPARABILITY: this 20-90% is a distance-graded TRANSFER haircut. It is NOT the same quantity as MKGSA's 10-25% recharge-credit haircut, which belongs with Merced's 10% Leave-Behind and East Turlock's 95% correction. Do not put them in one sentence.
