records.subsection: Transfer regime - inter-GSA
records.finding: FIRST EXPRESS INTER-GSA ALLOCATION TRANSFER MECHANISM FOUND IN THIS STUDY. EKGSA landowners may transfer Native Allocation for use in another GSA within the Kaweah Subbasin, and may receive the equivalent from another GSA, subject to approval by both the transferring and receiving GSA. In a three-GSA basin whose GSAs run materially different allocation methods, this is also the point at which those differences become arbitrageable.
records.direct_quote: "Eligible Landowners may transfer (i) all or any portion of their Native Allocation for use in another groundwater sustainability agency within the Subbasin, and (ii) the equivalent of EKGSA’s Native Allocation from another groundwater sustainability agency within the Subbasin for use on Eligible Land in EKGSA." (EKGSA Rules and Regulations Sec 3.01(e)(3), PDF 6)
records.notes: Within EKGSA: Native Allocation, Transitional Pumping and Groundwater Credits are transferable on an Agency form approved by the Executive Director; Rainfall Credits may NOT be transferred; transferred Transitional Pumping must be used within the Allocation Year and within EKGSA boundaries; all transfers subject to final Agency review "to avoid potential Undesirable Results" (PDF 6).

records.subsection: Allocation market - status and design
records.finding: THE ONLY OPERATING GROUNDWATER TRADING MARKET IN THIS STUDY. Originated in a 2019 USBR WaterSMART grant to TID; consultant Stantec; ~$800,000 total cost, ~50% USBR-funded; an 11-member Water Marketing Strategy Committee meeting since mid-2021 and including a member from Self-Help Enterprises; TWO PILOT AUCTIONS held May and June 2024 with an automated trading platform built into the Water Dashboard; trade volumes capped for the pilot; results published with landowner names removed.
records.direct_quote: "The Committee has established the initial elements of the Strategy. The Final Strategy will be informed by the completed pilot market. Two Pilot Market auctions took place in May and June 2024. During the Pilot Market, the MKGSA incorporated an automated trading platform into the Water Dashboard, allowing growers to seamlessly use the tool that has been developed for tracking and monitoring their individual water use." (MKGSA GSP Sec 6.7.3.1, PDF 394, printed p.6-57)
records.notes: The GSAs are explicit that the market moves water without creating any: "While such a program will not add to the GSA’s overall groundwater balance/budget, it may encourage the distribution of allocations in the most economically efficient manner" (Sec 6.7.3.5, PDF 395).

records.subsection: Water savings from repurposing - calculation
records.finding: No water-saving calculation, method, figure or target attaches to the $10M MLRP anywhere in the document set. For fallowing generally the calculation is not performed - the ledger simply stops debiting. GKGSA does not compute a saving; EKGSA converts fallowed acreage into ET Credit Acreage rather than into a stated volume. A genuinely different design from all four prior basins: Merced and East Turlock produce a NUMBER and then argue about it; Kaweah produces no number because not pumping shows up as not being debited.
records.direct_quote: The Kaweah MLRP's only published quantities are "an estimated 238 acres of retired irrigation land" and "65+ acres for habitat and community/tribal use" (EKGSA GSP PDF 1942). Word-boundary search of all 12,984 pages returns no acre-foot figure, demand-reduction estimate or water-benefit target associated with MLRP, land repurposing, or any of the three MLRP-funded project names.
records.notes: Whether the no-number design is better or worse is a real question for the DWR recommendation: it is self-verifying and needs no programme-specific measurement, but it also means the programme can never report what it achieved.

records.subsection: Accounting integration - recharge to allocation
records.finding: The clearest statement of accounting integration in the basin, and a complete measure-to-credit-to-allocate cycle. Allocations are re-set annually each July on the prior year's MEASURED recharge, above a stated sustainable yield of 0.83 AF/acre.
records.direct_quote: "Above the sustainable yield of 0.83 AF/acre, the MKGSA in coordination with the landowners, agreed that only water put into the groundwater system could be allocated into the future and the allocation was based on water recharged by TID in WY 2023. This new methodology for allocation has been widely promoted by the MKGSA and is considered “what you put into the groundwater system is what you get to take out or allocate.”" (MKGSA GSP Sec 6.7.1.1, PDF 389, printed p.6-52)
records.notes: Companion statement, same page: "It is important to acknowledge that MKGSA’s allocation system is not reliant on overdraft pumping but relies upon recharged groundwater supplies. MKGSA allocates only sustainable yield; therefore, the GSA does not have an “allowable overdraft” policy in its current allocation program."

records.subsection: Co-benefit quantification
records.finding: No co-benefit is measured, scored, rated, priced or verified anywhere in the Kaweah document set. No scoring rubric (contrast Merced's weighted checkbox), no differentiated per-acre rate schedule (contrast East Turlock's $730-$1,590 ladder), no ecological monitoring protocol (contrast East Turlock's Quick Assessment), no ecological threshold method (contrast Salinas Valley's per-GDE NDVI threshold), no DAC siting screen (contrast Merced's buffers). Kaweah is the weakest basin in the study on co-benefit quantification and holds the largest MLRP grant in it.
records.direct_quote: "This basin would also be combined with other potential project benefits such as habitat restoration or disadvantaged community drinking water benefits." - identical conditional wording at MKGSA GSP Sec 6.6.17.1 (PDF 381) and Sec 6.6.18.1 (PDF 383). No quantity, metric, protocol or verification attaches to either.
records.notes: One partial exception, labelled carefully: the Flying Dragon conservation easement is a DURABILITY instrument of the Merced Managed Wetland Method 2 kind - it locks the land use without measuring the ecological outcome. Per Open Questions #34 and #39, conditionality is not measurement.

records.subsection: Recurring funding for the accounting system
records.finding: CROSS-CHAPTER CONTRAST. MKGSA's accounting platform and administration run on a $10/AF administrative fee on all groundwater used in the GSA, with growers lacking surface water additionally paying $150-$200/AF for replacement water, and allocations and rates re-evaluated annually each July. records.subsection: Dust accounting
records.finding: SHARPEST DUST FINDING IN THE STUDY. Five basins, zero field-scale dust accounting - and Kaweah is the first where a BINDING RULE actively requires the condition that produces dust. The rule granting the consumptive-use exemption for fallowing simultaneously requires the landowner to suppress vegetation on the fallowed parcel, and the same rulebook contains no dust, air-quality or cover provision of any kind. The requirement is hydrologically rational - vegetation would register ET and defeat the exemption - and that is exactly why it matters: the ET-ledger design creates an affirmative incentive to keep repurposed land bare.
records.direct_quote: "All parcels must be maintained to limit the growth of any vegetation." (GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R Sec 4.03(e) Fallowed Lands, PDF 17)

records.subsection: Why acquisition-based repurposing is rare

records.subsection: Meaningful benefits - definition and measurement
records.finding: No meaningful-benefit definition, field, test or measurement exists anywhere. Unlike East Turlock, whose GSP Chapter 8 carries a required 'Benefits to Disadvantaged Communities' field for each of 29 projects and management actions, the Kaweah GSPs' project templates have NO DAC benefit field at all - as in Merced and Salinas Valley. Project co-benefits are stated in the conditional and none is quantified.
records.direct_quote: The nearest equivalent in the document set is a purpose statement written by a commenter: the Kaweah MLRP is "committed to the selection and implementation of multibenefit projects that reduce reliance on groundwater while supporting a viable agricultural economy and improving community and environmental health outcomes" (EKGSA GSP PDF 1942, Comment column). Word-boundary search of the three GSP project-description templates (Sec 6.6 in each) returns no DAC-benefit field, community-benefit field, or equivalent structural slot.

records.subsection: Distributional - community management area
records.finding: SHARPEST DISTRIBUTIONAL FINDING IN THE BASIN, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL. GKGSA's binding Fifth Amended Rules and Regulations carry Section 4.04 Community Management Areas reading, in full, '[To be determined]' - immediately followed by Section 4.05, a fully drafted and operative Special Uses Management Area for lands where dairies and processing plants are situated. EKGSA's equivalent is bare enabling authority. Both GSAs reserve a management-area mechanism for communities; in one it is a placeholder and in the other a bare power, while the equivalent mechanism for dairies is adopted and operative in the same document.
records.direct_quote: GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R, PDF 18, two consecutive sections. Section 4.04 is headed Community Management Areas and its entire body reads: "[To be determined]". Section 4.05 is headed Special Uses Management Area and reads: "A separate management area (“Special Uses Management Area”) shall be established for the purpose of accounting for certain water users. The area shall be comprised of lands where dairies and processing plants, are situated (hereinafter “Special use Parcels”)." EKGSA's equivalent, in full: "3.02. Community Management Areas. The Board may from time to time establish community management areas." (EKGSA R&R Sec 3.02, PDF 6)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-2): no document on disk states what a Community Management Area would do, who would qualify, or whether any has been proposed. The finding recorded is the blankness itself - do not infer intent in either direction. "[To be determined]" is the East Turlock "Transfer" pattern (Open Question #80) applied to the COMMUNITY provision.

records.subsection: Procedural access - standing extended to tenants
records.finding: FIRST EXTENSION OF AN ENTITLEMENT BEYOND OWNERS IN FIVE BASINS. Tenants receive interim drinking water supplies independent of land or well ownership, and the Plan tells them whom to contact to advocate with their landlord. Merced's appeal and variance standing runs to landowners only; MIUGSA extends to lessees and easement holders; ETSGSA to Owner or Operator where Operator includes a lessee. Kaweah is the first to name TENANTS, and to name them in the entitlement rather than in the procedure.
records.direct_quote: "A mitigation agreement will be made with the landowner; however, tenants shall receive interim drinking water supplies, independent of land/well ownership. For questions on the claims process or tenant questions on advocating for mitigation support with your landlord(s), please contact MKGSA and/or Self-Help Enterprises." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 3.1, PDF 30, printed p.22)
records.notes: State the asymmetry honestly: the mitigation AGREEMENT is still with the landowner; the tenant gets interim supplies, not the permanent fix.

records.subsection: Distributional - eligibility conditioned on claimant compliance
records.finding: Mitigation eligibility is conditioned on the claimant's own compliance with the allocation system: a claimant whose groundwater use has contributed to overdraft after 1 January 2015, such as by extracting more than their native yield allocation, does not qualify. Defensible in principle, and a real interaction between an accounting rule and an equity remedy - the kind of interaction a platform recommendation should surface.
records.direct_quote: "To qualify for MKGSA funding reimbursement, the impact must be (1) induced by groundwater overdraft conditions and (2) having occurred after January 1, 2015. In addition, if the Claimant’s groundwater use is contributing to or has contributed to overdraft (after January 1, 2015), such as extracting more than their native yield allocation, then they shall not qualify for mitigation support from the MKGSA." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 3.2.5, PDF 37, printed p.29)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-3): this appears in the TECHNICAL-ASSISTANCE track. Whether the same condition applies to the DRINKING-WATER track is not stated on that page - the drinking-water qualification criteria are in Figure 6, which is an image and was not read. NOT RESOLVED, and it matters: it determines whether a household's drinking-water remedy can be withheld on the basis of its own pumping.

records.subsection: Domestic well protection - proactive targeting
records.finding: KAWEAH OPERATES A PROACTIVE, RISK-TARGETED PROGRAMME FOR SMALL COMMUNITY WELLS, SELECTED BY A STATE RISK METRIC - no other basin in this study does. The Small Community Well Proactive & Protective Action Program (PPAP) selects wells identified at-risk by SWRCB metrics and delivers contingency planning, engineering reports for communities stuck for lack of funding, additional technical assistance, and - third in its list of four named measures - groundwater pumping restriction policies near at-risk community wells.
records.direct_quote: "The small community wells identified as being at-risk by the State Water Resources Control Board’s metrics for small community wells will receive mitigation in the form of proactive technical assistance/mitigation via the PPAP which is developed in conjunction with the Kaweah Subbasin Mitigation Program and GSA Mitigation Plans." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 2.4.1, PDF 26, printed p.18)
records.notes: Stated rationale, same page: "after consultations with local community well mitigation providers, it was determined the most effective and helpful mitigation for small community wells is to avoid the need for mitigation altogether." PPAP is IN DEVELOPMENT; its five phases are in Attachment A, not separately located, and no enrolled community appears in any document on disk.

records.subsection: Exposure analysis wired into the allocation
records.finding: TIGHTEST COUPLING BETWEEN A GROUNDWATER ACCOUNTING SYSTEM AND AN EQUITY REMEDY FOUND ANYWHERE IN THIS PROJECT. A Kaweah Subbasin Dry Well Susceptibility Analysis sized a $1.55 million minimum Mitigation Cost Reserve covering physical well mitigation, emergency and interim supplies, SHE administration, GSA administration and contractor assistance - and the reserve is refilled by setting the annual groundwater allocation. Compare Merced, whose Domestic Well Mitigation Program is Prop 218-funded with a $200,000 annual and $800,000 total cap and which did not deliver the interim-milestone exposure analysis its GSP promised (Open Question #143).
records.direct_quote: "The Mitigation Cost Reserves have a target minimum level of $1.55 million, which was determined from the Kaweah Subbasin Dry Well Susceptibility Analysis. The Mitigation Cost Reserves will be replenished annually by setting future annual allocations of groundwater to replenish the fund to the minimum target." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 5, PDF 44, printed p.36)
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-4): the Dry Well Susceptibility Analysis itself is NOT on disk - "More information on this analysis will be available in the 2024 Amended GSP upon adoption". Whether it disaggregates exposure by DAC status is undetermined. Per the Colusa Sec 3.1.4 precedent this pass does NOT perform a DAC/exposure join and does NOT assert the analysis lacks one.

records.subsection: Language access - written commitments
records.finding: KAWEAH DEPARTS FROM THE FOUR PRIOR BASINS: translation is committed in writing in a binding-adjacent instrument, not merely aspirational, and the Plan practises it - its claim-initiation page is printed in English and Spanish with the same SHE phone number and intake URL. Cross-basin framing: Merced's engagement innovations sat in a voluntary grant programme while its mandatory regulatory programme had none; Kaweah's sit in a MITIGATION PLAN, while both allocation rulebooks contain zero language, translation or outreach provisions. Same pattern, host instrument one step closer to the regulatory core.
records.direct_quote: "GSAs must develop and keep an updated page on their respective websites that outlines the Kaweah Subbasin Mitigation Program and their individual GSA Mitigation Plan. Materials explaining the process, mitigation and the application will be housed on this website page and accessible in English and Spanish." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 3.1.1, PDF 32, printed p.24)
records.notes: Companion commitments on the same page: "Outreach will be provided in multiple languages as determined appropriate by the GSA" and "At least one workshop shall be held in the MKGSA, preferably in an underrepresented community in English and Spanish translation services available." Three qualifications are in the text: "as determined appropriate" is discretionary, "preferably" is a preference, and translation services available is not live interpretation.

records.subsection: Dry well mitigation - proactive notification

records.notes: Companion statement at Sec 2.4.3, PDF 27: "The effectiveness of the Plan will be improved with a notification activation process, intended to notify well users and owners of groundwater conditions nearing the possibility of potential adverse impacts to their well." The process is Table 1 of the Plan.

records.subsection: Water quality - public informational layer
records.finding: THE STUDY'S BEST WORKED EXAMPLE OF THE PUBLIC, NO-LOGIN COMMUNITY INFORMATIONAL LAYER THIS PROJECT DEFINES AS THE GAP COMMUNITY USE CASE (standing rule, Open Question #47). records.subsection: Water quality - connection to accounting and siting

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.subsection: Domestic well data - voluntary registration and the trust problem
records.finding: MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL FINDING IN THIS BASIN, AND THE MOST TRANSFERABLE GAP FINDING IN THE KAWEAH MATERIAL. The same voluntary Well Registration Program is the designated fix for the missing per-well input to the ISW depletion calculation, the designated source of at-risk-well identification for the Mitigation Program, and the stated precondition for per-household water-quality alerting. Three separate accounting and equity functions depend on residents voluntarily disclosing private well data to a public agency - and the GSAs have written down that they expect residents to refuse.
records.direct_quote: "The GSAs are expecting there to be initial hesitation out of concern for the landowners’ private data to become public and impact property values and future economic opportunities." (MKGSA Mitigation Plan Sec 2.4.4, PDF 28, printed p.20)
records.notes: The reciprocity offered is named on the same page: "early risk notifications, reduced risk as GSAs will use this information to adapt management policies, and improvements in the GSAs’ groundwater level and quality analyses which inform sustainability planning." Registration is not a prerequisite for mitigation qualification but "if a well is registered it may be possible to apply for mitigation before the well goes dry."

records.subsection: DAC identification - method used instead of a state tool
records.finding: Kaweah does not use DWR's DAC Mapping Tool. DACs are identified from 2016 US Census Bureau Median Household Income criteria at Census Designated Place, Census Tract and Block Group level - and then corrected in one case by a community door-to-door survey. Compare Merced and Salinas Valley, which both use the DWR DAC Mapping Tool, and note that Merced's DAC source data was 11-25 years old (2026-08-04 Working Log).
records.direct_quote: "Data published by the U.S. Census Bureau (Bureau) in 2016 show ten areas within the jurisdiction of the GKGSA that meet the annual Median Household Income (MHI) criteria to be considered a Disadvantaged Community (DAC) or severely disadvantaged community (SDAC)." records.notes: 2016 Census data in a November 2024 plan is eight years old at adoption - better than Merced's but still a disclosed-but-unacknowledged currency gap.

records.subsection: Two-tier platform architecture
records.finding: KAWEAH IS THE FIRST BASIN IN THIS STUDY TO HAVE BUILT BOTH TIERS OF THE ARCHITECTURE THE PROJECT'S STANDING GAP RULE ANTICIPATES (Open Question #47). The transactional tier is the Water Dashboard (gsawd.com) and EKGSA's Credit Manager - login-based, landowner-facing, carrying allocations, monthly ET usage, invoicing and the pilot trading module, supported by twice-weekly clinics. records.subsection: Accounting platform carrying an equity instrument
records.finding: CLEAREST INSTANCE IN THIS STUDY OF AN ACCOUNTING PLATFORM CARRYING AN EQUITY INSTRUMENT AS A PRODUCT FEATURE. One of EKGSA's four 2024 direct mailers is itemised as announcing surface water credits for sale, also known as the Mitigation Tier - a named link between the allocation platform and mitigation funding, surfaced to landowners through the mail.
records.direct_quote: EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report PDF 5. The panel heading reads 4 DIRECT MAILERS SENT TO OVER 2,000 LANDOWNERS and the four itemised subjects are: "Announcement of surface water credits for sale, also known as the Mitigation Tier"; "New Credit Manager features starting with Allocation Year 2023 invoicing"; "Changes to supply for Allocation Year 2025"; "Urgent policy announcement regarding water credits and overdraft fees". Reproduced item by item because a second infographic column (WEBSITE BLOG POSTS / EMAIL NOTICES / OVER 2,000 VIEWS) interleaves with the list in every extraction.
records.notes: HUMAN REVIEW (U-6): no definition, rate, eligibility rule or accounting treatment for a Mitigation Tier appears in the EKGSA Rules and Regulations (April 2023) or anywhere else on disk - unsurprising, since the rulebook predates the mailer by a year. A live instrument documented only in a newsletter.

records.subsection: What benefits to habitat, dis-advantaged communities, local economies, etc. are considered?
records.finding: Water quality is a named, unmeasured MLRP co-benefit. GSP §8.1.1.1.4 lists it as a qualitative expectation of MA1 (reduced nutrient loading from fallowing; improved runoff quality from wetland habitat creation), while the only MA1 benefit the GSP quantifies is volumetric (C2VSimTM simulations, p. 8-11 [PDF 505]). Three Implementation Standards (Stormwater Ponds, Constructed Basins, Rewilding; p. 1 of each) and the 2026 Application §2.2 DOC desired-outcome checkbox ('Improved water quality') repeat it as a potential benefit.
records.direct_quote: "Degraded water quality – Fallowing of crop lands is expected to reduce agricultural water use and associated nutrient loading, and wetland habitat creation is expected to improve the quality of surface runoff, thereby improving groundwater quality." — GSP §8.1.1.1.4, p. 8-10 [PDF 504]
records.notes: Replaces the MLRP Benefits Matrix's 'Not found' rating for East Turlock water quality (now Named). Other benefit statements: Stormwater Ponds Standard p. 1 [PDF 1] (sedimentation and natural filtration of stormwater; reduced sediment and nutrient loads downstream); Constructed Basins Standard p. 1 [PDF 1]; Rewilding Standard p. 1 [PDF 1]; 2026 Application §2.2, p. 6 [PDF 6] (no page footer; page inferred from sequence); GSP §8.2, p. 8-55 [PDF 549] (GRAT being refined to site MLRP projects for benefits incl. water quality; refinement not reported in the WY 2025 Annual Report); GSP §8.3.3.7.4 Project 18, p. 8-123 [PDF 617]. Parallel nutrient-loading statements for non-MLRP Management Actions 2 (PDF 510) and 3 (PDF 513). Whether the §2.2 checkbox feeds scoring is unknown — ETSGSA scoring criteria unpublished (OQ #176). | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).

records.subsection: How are those co-benefits tracked and quantified?
records.finding: No MLRP water-quality metric, constituent, sampling requirement, threshold or verification exists in any ETSGSA MLRP instrument, GSP Chapter 8, Appendix K or the WY 2025 Annual Report. The Implementation Monitoring Plan contains no water-quality term, and every Annual Report water-quality hit belongs to the Degraded Water Quality sustainability indicator.
records.direct_quote: Word-boundary searches (2026-10-05) for 'water quality' / 'nitrate' / 'salinity' / 'contaminant' / 'constituent' / 'filtration' / 'runoff'. 12 ETSGSA MLRP documents: 6/0/0/0/0/2/29 (controls habitat 68, groundwater 366, MLRP 156). Implementation Monitoring Plan alone: 0 on all seven (controls 11/18/7). GSP Chapter 8 [PDF 495–664]: 24/1/0/2/0/0/43 (controls 15/1068/55). Appendix K [PDF 1350–1402]: 7/0/0/0/0/0/12 (controls 2/433/55). WY 2025 Annual Report: 47/21/2/23/7/0/2 (controls 1/1022/39). Every hit inspected; 0 classed as an MLRP water-quality metric or monitoring requirement.
records.notes: Outreach & Engagement Plan has no text layer and was searched via OCR; near-blank pages in the TechMemo, Monitoring Plan and Annual Report were rendered and OCR'd (flowcharts, dividers, maps). The process flowchart returns 0 for the controls, so its zeros carry little weight. Earthwork Standard SWPPP / Qualified Stormwater Professional monitoring (pp. 3–4) classed as construction-permit compliance, not benefit monitoring (OQ #177). Constructed Basins p. 8 inflow water-quality guidance is 'recommended but not required' design guidance. Row 139's 'ten' instruments are not enumerated; this search covered 12 (OQ #178). Hit counts as logged in the verification pass. | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?
records.finding: The Development Project Application rubric has nine scored categories: four Priority Criteria Categories — Merced Water Quality and Supply (35), Disadvantaged Community Benefits (25), Agricultural and Economic Resiliency (25), Regional Ecological Benefits (25) — and five Additional Criteria — Geographic Prioritization (25), Feasibility and Cost-Effectiveness (20), Proposed Wildlife Corridor (5), Regional Coordination (5), Additional Considerations (5). They sum to 170 points (our sum; no total is stated). A project must address at least one Priority element to be considered.
records.direct_quote: "To be considered for funding, projects must address at least one element in at least one of the Priority Criteria Categories listed below." — Application p. 10 [PDF 18]
records.notes: The Application is bound inside Merced_MLRP_RFP.pdf at PDF 9–31; printed page = PDF − 8. Category pages: p. 11–19 [PDF 19–27]. 'Additional Considerations' is headed 'Additional Criteria and Considerations' on its own page (OQ #181). Water Quality and Supply is the highest-weighted category (35 of 170). | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).

records.subsection: How are those co-benefits tracked and quantified?
records.finding: The 35-point 'Merced Water Quality and Supply' category's water-quality criterion requires improvement that can be measured and demonstrated, but names no constituent, unit or method; footnote 5 leaves the method to the applicant's narrative. Because full points can be earned by addressing a single criterion, the category can be maxed on supply criteria alone.
records.direct_quote: "Water Quality Benefits: Provides improvement in water quality that can be measured and demonstrated." — Application p. 11 [PDF 19]
records.notes: Footnote 5, verbatim: "If you are able to describe methods of measurement or observation, please add that information into this category's narrative." (p. 11 [PDF 19]). Corrects the MLRP Benefits Matrix paraphrase 'water-quality/supply benefit category'. | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).

records.subsection: What benefits to habitat, dis-advantaged communities, local economies, etc. are considered?
records.finding: 'Agricultural and Economic Resiliency (25 Points)' is a Priority category with three criteria: Supports Sustainability of Local Agriculture; Sustains Agricultural Economies; Diversifies Economic Opportunities. Its job criterion is framed around minimizing agricultural job displacement and improving farmworker conditions. No metric attaches to any criterion.
records.direct_quote: "Sustains Agricultural Economies: Minimizes agricultural job displacement or provides other economic benefits including increased pay, benefits, job security, and/or working conditions for farmworkers." — Application p. 13 [PDF 21]
records.notes: Corrects the MLRP Benefits Matrix paraphrase 'ag/economic resiliency'. | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).

records.subsection: Is there an accounting system for integration of these co-benefits?
records.finding: Water quality and job displacement are each scored in two categories. Disadvantaged Community Benefits (25 points) carries a DAC drinking-water/water-quality criterion and an 'Economic and Workforce Benefits' criterion that includes mitigation of job displacement, alongside the Water Quality and Supply and Agricultural and Economic Resiliency categories. The rubric has no rule against scoring one benefit in two categories.
records.direct_quote: "Economic and Workforce Benefits: Provides economic and workforce opportunities for members of disadvantaged communities, improves access to support services, and/or mitigation of job displacement." — Application p. 12 [PDF 20]
records.notes: Confirms row 49's 'mitigation of job displacement' wording and locates it in Disadvantaged Community Benefits, not Agricultural and Economic Resiliency. The DAC water-quality criterion is headed 'Drinking Water Supply and Security Benefits and/or Water Quality Benefits for Disadvantaged Communities' (same page). Whether scorers award the same benefit in both categories is not stated. | Added 2026-10-05 MLRP-matrix verification pass (CLAUDE.md OQ #176–#182).
